text: 'In history, where kindness is the rarest of pearls, the man who is kindly almost takes precedence of the man who is great.' Marius, a few Books ago, worshipped Napoleon's greatness. Which does this book, so far, seem to value more?

title: Nobody to blame
text: Hugo insists the coming conflicts were nobody's crime: the king defends royalty in good faith, democracy attacks in good faith, 'a blind man is no more a criminal than a Vendean is a ruffian'. It is a generous position, and a deliberate one: he wants us to watch the struggle without simple villains.

title: To produce wealth and to share it
text: Hugo reduces the socialist thinkers of the 1830s, Saint-Simon, Fourier and others, to two problems: producing wealth and distributing it. England, he says, solves the first and fails the second; communism kills production to divide it. His own answer is to make property 'universal' and education free and compulsory.

title: Piles of shadows
text: The chapter ends in weather: shadows gathering on the horizon, leaves trembling 'at the approach of a storm', cholera, risings at Lyon, the Duchesse de Berry stirring the Vendée. Hugo has used storm imagery for the inner life of his characters. Now the whole country has a tempest in its skull.

title: History from police files
text: Hugo builds this chapter out of overheard remarks, secret reports, torn letters, a recipe for gunpowder found in a drawer. It reads like a dossier. The method makes the insurrection feel like something that grew out of a thousand small acts by ordinary people, not a plan drawn up by a few.

title: How is your wife?
text: Shopkeepers ask workmen 'How is the rising coming along?' in the tone of 'How is your wife?' A furniture dealer offers his gun. The strangest thing Hugo records is how public and calm it all was: an insurrection preparing 'in the face of the government'.

title: The barbarians of civilization
text: Hugo defends the ragged crowds of 1793 from the Faubourg Saint-Antoine: they 'demanded light with the mask of night'. Between them and the gilded men 'glorifying ... the sword, the stake, and the scaffold', he would choose the barbarians. Then he adds a third way: 'progress with a gentle slope'.

title: The Faubourg Saint-Antoine
text: The working-class district east of the Bastille had supplied the crowds of 1789 and 1793 and was the traditional heart of Parisian revolt. Hugo calls it 'that powder-house of suffering and ideas'. The Friends of the A.B.C. appear here too, briefly, as one small cell in a much larger network.

title: A census of the willing
text: Enjolras sends each friend to a different corner of Paris, the polytechnic students, the masons, the medical school, the law courts, and keeps the Cougourde for himself. Hugo uses the roll-call to show the reach of the movement and to remind us who each young man is. Marius, 'that abstracted Marius', is the one name missing.

title: I believe in you
text: 'You do not believe in everything.' 'I believe in you.' Grantaire volunteers for the Barrière du Maine, puts on a red Robespierre waistcoat and whispers 'Be easy.' Enjolras finds him playing dominoes. The joke is sharp, but Grantaire's one faith, in a person rather than a principle, is plain.

title: Fanning the ashes
text: The workmen of the Barrière du Maine are 'becoming extinguished'; 'those ashes must be fanned into a glow'. Enjolras pictures his friends as a 'powder train' and an 'electric spark', and sees 'a luminous uplifting beneath the gloomy skirts of the future'. For him, revolution is fire and light.

title: The wicked poor man
text: Marius flees the Gorbeau house partly from horror at what he saw there, 'a social deformity which is, perhaps, even more terrible than the wicked rich man, the wicked poor man'. After all of Hugo's pleading for the poor, the phrase is a hard one. It admits that misery can produce monsters without excusing the society that made them.

title: Five francs every Monday
text: Marius borrows money for the first time in his life, from Courfeyrac, to send five francs a week to Thénardier in La Force. 'Whence can this come to me?' Thénardier wonders. The son honours his father's debt to the man he just saw torture a prisoner. Is this loyalty, or a refusal to look at what he knows?

title: Thought and reverie
text: 'Thought is the toil of the intelligence, reverie its voluptuousness. To replace thought with reverie is to confound a poison with a food.' Hugo warns that a poor man who is generous and does not work slides down a slope that ends in 'suicide or crime'. It is a sober passage about a hero the narrator plainly loves.

title: Writing to her
text: Marius fills a notebook with his purest reveries and calls it 'writing to her'. He does not even know her name: not Ursule, and 'the Lark' is only a nickname he heard from a criminal. Love, Hugo says, 'kindles in the darkness of the heart; the more it has disappeared, the more it beams'.

title: The Lark's meadow
text: A passer-by names a pretty field by the Bièvre 'the Lark's meadow' and adds that Ulbach murdered a shepherdess there, a real crime of 1827. Marius hears only the first word. 'It was absurd, but irresistible.' A place-name becomes a shrine, much as a handkerchief's initials did before.

title: His heroic and his equivocal sides
text: Marius now thinks the white-haired workman near the Invalides was M. Leblanc in disguise. Why did he not cry out? Why did he flee the police? Is he the girl's father at all? The reader can answer some of these questions. Marius cannot, and they do not diminish his love.

title: Loose ends
text: Hugo lists what Javert's triumph missed: the victim fled, Montparnasse slipped away with Éponine, and Claquesous vanished from a police carriage between the Gorbeau house and La Force. The chapter is an accounting of escapes. The underworld leaks out of every net the law throws.

title: Paws in crime and paws in authority
text: Did Claquesous melt into the shadows, or did some police agent let him go because 'such a villain ... might make a very good agent'? Hugo raises the possibility that order and disorder are 'on such intimate juggling terms with the night'. Vidocq, remember, was a convict before he was a policeman. The line between hunter and hunted is not as clean as Javert believes.

title: Brujon, 1811
text: A fortress carved with a nail on the wall of La Force, signed 'Brujon, 1811', by the father of the Brujon of 1832. Crime here runs in families like a trade. Hugo has spent this volume on fathers and sons; this is the darkest version of the inheritance.

title: A postilion into Ireland
text: Hugo enjoys the prison slang: a 'postilion' is a pellet of bread with a message inside, thrown over the roofs from one yard to another, 'into Ireland'. A 'biscuit' means 'nothing to be done'. The note passes from Brujon to Babet to a woman in the Salpêtrière to Magnon to Éponine, a whole postal service of the underworld.

title: A gate on a garden
text: 'Babet. There is an affair in the Rue Plumet. A gate on a garden.' Éponine goes to look, watches the house for days, and sends back a biscuit: nothing to be done. What did she see there that made her call the job off?

title: Knotting another thread
text: 'Often when we think we are knotting one thread, we are tying quite another.' Hugo ends on a proverb about unintended consequences. The book has been full of small acts, a coin given, a coat left behind, a note tossed through a wall, that change things in ways nobody planned.

title: When misery looses bonds
text: Marius and Mabeuf pass on the boulevard with a melancholy nod and do not speak. 'There comes a moment when misery looses bonds! Two men who have been friends become two chance passersby.' Poverty isolates. Mabeuf, nearly eighty, now eats one egg a day and gives the other to his unpaid servant.

title: A tear of dew
text: Too weak to draw water from his well, Mabeuf looks up at a sky full of stars and begs for 'A tear of dew! A little pity!' The stars are beautiful and useless. Then a voice in the hedge offers help. Hugo's light imagery turns practical here: what the old man needs is not radiance but rain.

title: Angel or devil
text: Éponine waters the whole garden, barefoot, looking like a bat among the flowerbeds. 'You are an angel since you take care of the flowers.' 'No. I am the devil, but that's all the same to me.' Mabeuf blesses her; she calls herself damned. Which of them is right?

title: A goblin of the Bièvre
text: Mabeuf has been reading old books on demons and the goblins said to haunt his very garden. Falling asleep, he wonders whether his visitor was one. Hugo lets the old bookman's superstition frame the scene, so Éponine, who appears and vanishes in the twilight, has something of a spirit about her.

title: Poorer and prettier
text: Éponine has grown 'poorer and prettier, two steps which it had not seemed within her power to take', 'towards the light and towards distress'. Straw in her hair from a stable loft, prison in her face, and yet 'she was beautiful'. Hugo will not let us see her only as the girl of the Gorbeau garret.

title: You have called me Éponine!
text: Marius uses her name to make her swear she will not tell her father the address. She hardly hears the oath. 'That's nice! You have called me Éponine!' To him the name is a tool; to her it is a gift. Few moments in the book show so clearly the gap between what each of them wants.

title: I don't want your money
text: He fumbles out his only coin, the five francs meant for her father in prison, and puts it in her hand. She lets it fall to the ground. She has told us she would sew his shirt, and asked to see him smile. The one thing she refuses is payment. What does she want instead?

title: A woman like me
text: 'A nice young man like you must not be seen with a woman like me.' Hugo pauses on the word 'woman' in the mouth of a child of not quite sixteen: 'No tongue can express all that lay in that word.' Marius, in ecstasy, notices nothing. The reader is made to notice everything he misses.

title: A house built to hide
text: The Rue Plumet house was made by an eighteenth-century judge to conceal a mistress: a back lodge to hide a child and nurse, a secret door, a walled lane winding a quarter of a league to the Rue de Babylone. Only the birds saw it. Hugo describes its architecture in detail because its whole design is concealment, and its new tenant has a great deal to conceal.

title: The narrator says it at last
text: 'This unobtrusive tenant was Jean Valjean, the young girl was Cosette.' Hugo confirms in his own voice what Thénardier shouted in the garret, and adds that the reader 'has, doubtless, been no less prompt than Thénardier' to see it. He kept the secret from Marius for a whole Book, but never really from us.

title: Happiness that might be theft
text: Valjean left the convent because he was too happy there. He saw that keeping Cosette among the nuns, letting a vocation 'germinate' in her before she knew life, would be 'to rob a human creature of its nature and to lie to God'. The man once condemned for theft now examines his own love for any trace of stealing. His conscience is still the sharpest thing about him.

title: The inseparable
text: Valjean carries a small valise with an 'odor of embalming' that he never lets out of his sight and never opens before others. Cosette laughs and says she is jealous of it. Hugo states the fact and offers no explanation.

title: Three addresses
text: Besides the Rue Plumet house, Valjean rents two poor rooms in distant quarters, the Rue de l'Ouest and the Rue de l'Homme Armé, so he can vanish at a moment's warning. 'This lofty virtue had three domiciles in Paris for the sake of escaping from the police.' The reader now understands the flat Marius found empty, and the sudden flights.

title: Better than the master
text: Cosette has the pavilion, the tapestries, the heated rooms; Valjean lives in the porter's lodge with a folding bed, no fire, and black bread. 'It is the young lady who is the mistress of this house.' 'And you, monsieur?' 'I am a much better thing than the master, I am the father.' Hugo shows love as self-denial in the smallest household details.

title: A convict in the National Guard
text: The census of 1831 swept 'M. Fauchelevent' into the National Guard, the citizen militia of the July Monarchy. Valjean mounts guard willingly: the uniform is 'a correct disguise which mixed him with everyone'. The escaped galley-slave now patrols for public order. 'Within, the angel, without, the bourgeois.'

title: Two costumes
text: With Cosette he dresses like a retired officer; alone, at night, he wears a workman's blouse and a cap over his face. 'Was this precaution or humility? Both.' The reader now knows what Marius glimpsed near the Invalides. Toussaint calls him a saint; her butcher calls him 'a queer fish'.

title: The benevolent gentleman
text: Valjean takes Cosette to Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas because it is far away, gives generously to the poor of that district, and so draws Thénardier's begging letter. Hugo ties the threads together: his charity is what led him into the trap. Goodness in this book is never safe.

title: The garden that belongs to itself
text: Left alone for half a century, the garden has become a thicket 'as impenetrable as a forest, as peopled as a city ... sombre like a cathedral'. Branches and weeds 'married' in 'the holy mystery of fraternity, symbol of the human fraternity'. Hugo makes the wild garden an image of what society might be if nothing blocked 'the sacred effort of things towards life'.

title: Nothing is small
text: The digression widens from a Paris garden to the whole cosmos: 'the radiation of the star profits the rose', a nebula is 'an anthill of stars', and the universe is 'a machine made of mind ... the prime motor of which is the gnat'. It is Hugo's mystical side. Notice how it echoes the book's moral claim that no person is too small to matter.

title: Paphos made over into Eden
text: A garden built for illicit love has 'returned to virginity and modesty' and is now 'arranged for love' of a purer kind. And 'there was, also, in this solitude, a heart which was quite ready'. Hugo is plainly setting a stage. The question is who will walk onto it.

title: Many mothers, no mother
text: 'All the nuns in the world are not worth as much as one mother in the formation of a young girl's soul.' Cosette had 'many mothers, in the plural', and an old man who 'knew nothing at all'. Hugo warns that convent ignorance leaves the heart to build its romances in the dark. It is one of his clearest statements about what a parent gives.

title: Black bread
text: 'If you eat it, I will eat it too.' So Valjean eats white bread to stop Cosette eating black. She scolds him for his cold room and threatens to visit until he lights a fire. The man who went to the galleys over a loaf now gives up his bread of penance for the girl he loves.

title: Perhaps this man is my mother
text: Cosette prays for a mother she never knew and does not even know her name; whenever she asks, Valjean is silent, and once the smile ends in a tear. 'This silence ... covered Fantine with darkness.' Cosette imagines her mother's soul has passed into the old man. The reader knows the name, and the story, that he cannot bring himself to say.

title: Through martyrdom
text: Cosette dreams of her mother with great wings and says she must have been 'almost a saint'. Valjean answers: 'Through martyrdom.' Is his silence about Fantine a kindness to Cosette, or a debt he is not paying?

title: The same story, from her side
text: Hugo now rewinds to the Luxembourg and tells it again through Cosette. We saw the thin girl become beautiful through Marius's eyes; now we see her discover it in a mirror. The chapter ends exactly where Marius's story began: 'It was at this epoch that Marius ... saw her once more at the Luxembourg.' The two halves click together.

title: She had just dazzled herself
text: Cosette, who was told she was ugly all her childhood, looks in the mirror and cries out. Her beauty arrives 'like the sudden advent of daylight'. The image picks up the light Marius saw around her bench. Notice the mirror: the Jondrette girl looked into one in Marius's room too.

title: What is to become of me?
text: 'How beautiful she is! What is to become of me?' Valjean watches her beauty with terror, because it means change in a life so happy he dares not move. Hugo names the difference plainly: 'What he beheld with anguish, a mother would have gazed upon with joy.' His love is a father's and also something more fearful.

title: He would lose by heaven
text: Valjean, still a fugitive whom 'the law had not released from its grasp', asks one thing of Providence, the law and the world: that Cosette go on loving him. Asked if he wanted heaven, 'he would have replied: I should lose by it.' The saintly man has one attachment he would not give up even for God.

title: That disguise
text: Valjean asks her to wear her old schoolgirl merino again. 'That disguise! ... I shall never put on those horrors again.' To him the plain clothes were safety; to her they were a costume she has outgrown. He himself has lived in disguises for years. Hugo lets the word land on him.

title: Two clouds laden with lightning
text: Hugo defends the much-mocked 'glance' of romance: 'That is the way people do fall in love, nevertheless, and the only way.' Cosette had noticed Marius long before he noticed her, and thought him handsome while he still thought her plain. Love here is mutual from the first, though neither knows it.

title: Timid boy, bold girl
text: 'The first symptom of true love in a young man is timidity; in a young girl it is boldness.' It was Cosette who led her father along the walk toward Marius's bench. The reader saw the moment from Marius's side as a miracle. From hers, it was a decision.

title: Love without a name
text: In the convent's song-books 'amour' was replaced by 'tambour' or 'pandour', so Cosette has no word for what she feels. 'Is anyone the less ill because one does not know the name of one's malady?' In a book obsessed with names, she loves without being able to name either the feeling or the man.

title: Stars separated by millions of leagues
text: 'They did not address each other ... they saw each other; and like stars of heaven ... they lived by gazing at each other.' The whole affair is conducted with the eyes. To Cosette, Marius is 'a vision', 'charming, luminous, and impossible'.

title: A dog scanning a thief
text: Valjean, who thought himself past malice, feels 'the old depths of his soul' open against Marius, 'craters forming in his bosom'. His long inward speech, sixty years on his knees, forgiven every evil, and now 'a great booby' at the Luxembourg, is self-pity and grief together. The convict's old wrath is not dead, only sleeping.

title: The traps Marius fell into
text: Now we learn what was behind the changed benches, the forgotten handkerchief, the visits alone: 'Jean Valjean laid a host of ambushes for him', and Marius 'answered yes' to every one. The 'three blunders' Hugo counted earlier were tests set by a jealous father. Cosette, meanwhile, gave nothing away.

title: What have I done?
text: Alone at night on his pallet, Valjean looks back at the convent as an Eden he left 'voluntarily and madly' and asks 'What have I done?' The choice he made out of conscience, to give Cosette the world, has brought the world to her gate. Self-sacrifice has turned on him.

title: Suffering side by side, with a smile
text: 'What is the matter with you?' 'There is nothing the matter with me.' 'And you, father?' 'With me? Nothing.' Two people who love each other completely now hide their pain from each other. Hugo makes the sadness lie in the kindness: neither will hurt the other by speaking.

title: Would you like to come to the Luxembourg?
text: Once, Cosette says yes and Marius is not there; the next day she says no. Her silence is a strategy her father cannot read. Is Valjean's ignorance of 'the only miseries which are charming' a failing, or simply the cost of a life with no youth in it?

title: A vision at daybreak
text: Hugo builds the chain-gang out of the dark like an apparition: a confused shape, wheels, the clank of something like chains, then faces turned to 'the faces of corpses' by the first light. We see it before we understand it, exactly as Cosette does. Then the sun rises and sets 'fire to all those ferocious heads'.

title: Twenty-four men to a chain
text: Iron collars, one chain for all, guards with cudgels flogging even the sick, children running behind 'screaming with laughter', an old woman telling her son 'let that be a warning to you!' Hugo calls it Dante's seven circles on the march. This is what the law does with the men Book VII called the products of ignorance and misery.

title: Five and thirty years before
text: Valjean cannot move his feet. He remembers that this is the usual route, chosen to keep the convoy out of the king's sight, and that he himself passed this barrier thirty-five years ago. The reader saw him leave Toulon. Here, for the first time in years, his past drives by in daylight with the woman he loves beside him.

title: Are they still men?
text: 'Father, are they still men?' 'Sometimes,' answers the unhappy man. That night Cosette says that if she met one of those men she would die at the sight. She has no idea what she is saying, or to whom. The single word 'sometimes' carries everything Valjean has lived.

title: Shelter in a uniform
text: To take Cosette's mind off the convicts, Valjean takes her to the public fêtes in his National Guard uniform, 'with the vague inward feeling of a man who is betaking himself to shelter'. Earlier he envied a general's gold lace. A uniform is the opposite of a convict's red blouse, and he hides inside it.

title: What are the galleys like?
text: Days later, on a sunny morning, Cosette pulls a daisy apart, 'without a suspicion that to pluck a daisy apart is to do the same by a heart', and asks over her shoulder: 'Father, what are the galleys like?' Hugo ends the chapter on the question, without an answer.

title: The burn, seen from home
text: The morning after the Gorbeau trap, Valjean appears 'calm as was his wont' with a burned arm he explains 'in some way or other', and refuses a doctor. The reader knows exactly how he got it. Hugo makes us see the heroic scene from the other side: at home it looks like a minor accident kept secret.

title: What a good misfortune!
text: Nursing him, Cosette returns to his lodge and reads to him, and his fears about the young man dissolve. 'Oh! what a kindly wound!' He even feels grateful to the Thénardiers. The torture they meant for him has given him back his daughter for a month.

title: Light falls into cellars
text: 'In spring, sad souls grow light, as light falls into cellars at midday.' April brings Cosette back to life without her noticing. Hugo ties the inner weather to the season, as he did when Marius first saw her change on a summer morning.

title: There is the sun
text: Mabeuf owes three quarters' rent, has no wood, no meat, no bread on credit. 'What will you warm yourself with this winter?' 'There is the sun.' His serenity is almost saintly and almost foolish. Gavroche, listening under the hedge, decides not to steal his apples.

title: The hardest of all work is thieving
text: Valjean pins Montparnasse to the ground and delivers a long sermon on idleness: the rolling-mill of crime, the rope of torn sheets, the hollowed sou with its watch-spring saw, twenty years in and out at fifty 'broken, bent ... with white locks'. He is describing his own life. The reader has seen the sou; Montparnasse has no idea who is speaking.

title: My purse? Here it is
text: The sermon ends with Valjean handing over his purse to the young thief, as the Bishop once handed over his candlesticks. 'The blockhead!' says Montparnasse. Hugo has shown us the gesture before. The question is whether it can work twice, on a different kind of man.

title: Fallen from heaven
text: Gavroche picks the purse from Montparnasse's pocket and throws it over the hedge to Mabeuf. The money passes from a saint to a thief to a street boy to a starving old man in a few minutes. 'That has fallen from heaven,' says Mother Plutarque. Providence in this book often works through the most unlikely hands.

title: Passion calmed or lulled to sleep
text: Spring heals Cosette faster than Marius. 'Why! I no longer think of him.' Hugo is blunt about the difference: Marius buries himself in sorrow, Cosette plunges in and comes out again. 'Whose fault was it? No one's.' It is an unusually unromantic observation from a romantic narrator.

title: The lancer again
text: The officer passing the gate every day, with waxed moustache and cigar, is Théodule Gillenormand, Marius's cousin, the aunt's favourite and the comic spy of Book III. Hugo enjoys the coincidence. Théodule, for his part, cannot be bothered to look at every girl who looks at him.

title: Marble column or wine-shop post
text: An orphan girl's heart is like a vine tendril that clings to whatever is nearest, 'the capital of a marble column or ... the post of a wine-shop'. Hugo warns that a poor unknown young man may be the column and a polished man of the world the post. The image asks the reader to judge suitors from the inside, as he asked us to judge Marius.
